sources.title: Reuters Apple earnings and memory outlook
Reuters Asia and global markets Nov 3

title: Who pays for memory? Apple beats expectations, suppliers gain leverage and markets question capital costs

summary.changed: Apple beat sales and EPS forecasts but warned of a holiday gross-margin decline on surging memory costs; US ISM rose to 55.5 while input inflation stayed elevated; US tech stocks fell; Treasury updated borrowing needs and Asia weakened.
summary.missed: Memory scarcity shifts pricing power toward suppliers but can also damage end demand. Falling Treasury yields are not automatically bullish if driven by credit and growth fears.
summary.watch: US midterms and JOLTS today, Treasury refunding Wednesday, payrolls Friday. Monitor MU, WDC, TLT, AI CAPEX and ROIC.

sections.heading: The central story: memory gets pricier, splitting the AI chain into winners and payers
paragraphs: Apple's November 2 results provide unusually clear evidence that a shortage of one component can redistribute profit across the AI supply chain. Quarterly sales were $114.48 billion versus LSEG consensus of $113.39 billion; nevertheless, management guided holiday-quarter gross margin down to 45%–46% from 47.9%, citing rising memory and AI-related costs. Sources: Reuters and Apple's SEC filing.

Our thesis: end-product vendors can deliver record sales while losing pricing power to memory suppliers. That supports a demand thesis for MU and memory producers but does not prove that every supplier's earnings will rise at the same rate.

sections.heading: Apple: an earnings beat paired with a margin warning
paragraphs: Revenue was $114.48 billion, roughly $1.09 billion or 0.96% above the $113.39 billion forecast. EPS was $2.10 versus $1.99 expected; management noted a $0.05 benefit from tariff refunds. iPhone revenue reached $57.58 billion versus $56.54 billion expected, according to Reuters on November 2.

Holiday-quarter services revenue growth is guided at 8%–9% versus 10.7% expected. The 45%–46% gross-margin outlook is about 2.4 percentage points below the reported quarter at the midpoint; this does not imply an identical decline in net profit.

Apple shares fell as much as 4% during the earnings call, then pared losses to roughly 2% in after-hours trade; neither is a regular-session closing price. Purchase commitments rose by $33 billion during the quarter, but management did not explicitly confirm a long-term memory supply contract.

sections.heading: MU, WDC and the memory chain: opportunity is not immunity
paragraphs: Reuters reported Micron up more than 1% in after-hours trading after Apple's remarks. This is a point-in-time move, not confirmation of improved long-term cash flows. Apple cited memory shortages and rising prices, but disclosed no direct MU ASP, volume or new-contract figures.

For WDC, distinguish hard drives, data-center storage and NAND memory: a DRAM or HBM shortage does not automatically improve disk-drive profitability. Track ASP, gross margins, inventories, long-term orders and capital spending.

sections.heading: Wall Street: a widening split between industrials and technology
paragraphs: On November 2 the S&P 500 fell 0.51% to 7,541.40, the Nasdaq lost 1.07% and the Dow gained 0.41%. Stocks reversed early gains as technology weakened. These are completed regular-session figures from Reuters, not premarket quotes.

Oracle fell nearly 9% following plans to raise $20 billion, while investors weighed the cost of funding AI infrastructure. Energy stocks fell about 4% as oil retreated. The market is shifting from rewarding growth alone toward scrutinizing debt, cash generation and capital costs.

sections.heading: ISM: stronger factories, persistent input-price inflation
paragraphs: October ISM manufacturing rose to 55.5 from 54.5 versus market expectations around 54.6, the tenth consecutive month above 50. Production advanced to 59.0 from 56.7, the highest since November 2021; new orders improved to 55.5 from 55.3.

The prices-paid index eased to 75.2 from 77.9, still an elevated reading. Employment slipped to 52.4 from 52.7. Strong demand alongside input inflation complicates the case for rapid monetary easing. Sources: ISM and Reuters.
Customer inventories stood at 41.6, classified as too low, while supplier deliveries were slow at 59.1. This may support future orders but can also intensify price pressures and bottlenecks.

sections.heading: US Treasuries, TLT and government financing
paragraphs: During November 2 trading the 10-year Treasury yield was quoted around 4.884% and the 30-year around 5.258%, according to market reports; these are trading indications, not official Treasury closing observations. Early November 3, the 10-year yield rebounded to around 4.913%, Reuters reported.

The Treasury reduced its fourth-quarter net borrowing estimate by $10 billion to $618 billion, but projects $800 billion in the first quarter of 2027. Part of the change reflects cash balances rather than a structural improvement in the deficit. Wednesday brings the quarterly refunding announcement.
Lower long yields generally support TLT, but sensitivity depends on duration, convexity and market conditions. No verified TLT return is presented here.

sections.heading: Asia: semiconductor equities sell off even as chip factories remain busy
paragraphs: On November 3 morning, MSCI Asia ex-Japan fell 1.4%, South Korea's KOSPI dropped as much as 4.1% and Taiwan shares fell 3.3%. These are Reuters intraday indications, not closing figures. Taiwan's market was about 13.1% below its early-October peak.

The likely concern is sustainability of the AI capital-spending cycle, not necessarily cancelled orders. Bank of America noted outflows from Korea and Taiwan, but no verified institutional buying data for individual securities is available.

sections.heading: Oil, Hormuz and inflation: a sharp fall followed by stabilization
paragraphs: After Monday's sharp fall, Brent traded around $105.30 a barrel early November 3, up roughly 0.5% intraday, Reuters reported. Iran-related negotiations and Hormuz disruptions remain uncertain; a report of US strikes on Qeshm Island is neither a peace agreement nor confirmation of fully restored shipping.

Sustained cheaper oil could ease inflation, while freight disruption and elevated energy prices still pressure industrial and electricity costs. A daily crude move cannot be mapped directly to drilling-company earnings without examining hedges and customer CAPEX budgets.

sections.heading: FX, Australian rates and the transmission of risk
paragraphs: Australia's central bank raised its cash rate 25 basis points to 4.85% in a split 6–3 vote. The Australian dollar slipped about 0.3% to US$0.6978, illustrating why a rate hike does not dictate a currency's direction.
No fresh USD/ILS quote was verified, so no daily shekel move is claimed. The global focus remains real rates, bond yields and US midterms.

sections.heading: Fund flows, ETFs and crypto: keep reporting windows separate
paragraphs: The latest verified global fund-flow figures cover the week ended October 28, not Monday: global equities +$10.19 billion, US equity funds −$6.65 billion and technology funds +$5.50 billion. They do not prove buying or selling on November 2.
No new independently verified IBIT or JEPQ closing prices or fund-specific flows were available in this research. Bitcoin volatility and the Binance hack cannot be treated as IBIT's daily return.

sections.heading: Contrarian view: markets may punish customers and reward suppliers too aggressively
paragraphs: Bull case: demand for memory and computing keeps expanding, supplier selling prices remain firm, and semiconductor cash flows improve even as their customers face margin pressure.

Bear case: rising memory costs force handset, PC and server makers to raise prices, reduce configurations or delay orders. The favorable supplier pricing cycle could then end earlier than expected. Monitor inventories, purchase commitments, ASP, returns on capital and underlying demand forecasts.

sections.heading: Catalysts: elections, JOLTS, Treasury refunding and payrolls
paragraphs: US midterm voting takes place November 3, with JOLTS also expected that day. The Treasury refunding announcement is due Wednesday November 4, and the October employment report Friday November 6. Distinguish forecasts and scheduled events from results not yet released.

Watch MU for memory pricing; WDC for storage demand and inventories; FPS/COHR/VRT for AI orders versus CAPEX and free cash flow; TLT for the long yield curve; and BHF for its separate deal-specific catalysts rather than inferring from tech-sector performance.

contrarian: Memory shortages can support supplier margins near term but delay end demand if consumer prices rise. Test ASP, inventories, free cash flow and ROIC against WACC.
bottom_line: The crucial Apple number is not record sales but the expected gross-margin decline caused by memory costs. The next AI winners will be determined by pricing power and capital returns, not growth alone.
disclaimer: Based on information available early November 3, 2026. Asian equity, oil and yield quotes are intraday, not closes. Not investment advice.
